title: Run a query, read the result

outcomes.can: Read a result table: its columns, its rows and its row count.
Find the line and the name a SQL error points at, and repair it.
Write a first query from a one-line request.

intro: A database keeps data in tables, and SQL is the language for asking questions about them. Every exercise in this course works the same way: you write a query, save the file, and read what comes back. This module covers that loop.

steps.title: Tables, rows and columns
steps.text: A table holds one kind of thing. The departments table has one row for each department and one column for each fact about it: id, name, location and budget. A query asks for data. SELECT name, location FROM departments; says which columns you want and which table they come from. The semicolon ends the statement. SQL keywords such as SELECT and FROM can be written in any case. This course writes them in capitals so they stand out from table and column names. When you save an exercise, your SQL runs on a fresh copy of the practice database, so nothing you do is kept between checks. The file schema.sql beside your answer lists every table and every row. This course uses PostgreSQL.

steps.title: Predict the shape of a result
steps.text: Read the query and predict how many columns and rows come back.

steps.title: Read the result table
steps.text: The first line of a result names the columns, in the order the query listed them. Each line after that is one row. The last line counts the rows. The query asked for two of the four columns, and the table has six departments, so the result is two columns wide and six rows long. The rows came back in the order they were stored. A query that does not ask for an order is not promised one, which a later module deals with.

steps.title: Predict an error
steps.text: One column name in this query is misspelled. Read it before checking.

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. PostgreSQL reports error 42703: column "locaton" does not exist. The numbers after the file name are the line and the character where it found the problem. Nothing is returned when a statement has an error. The message often includes a hint with the name it thinks you meant. Start reading at the line it names.

steps.title: Repair a query
steps.text: Save the starter as it is and read the error. Fix what it names and save again. There is more than one mistake.

steps.title: List the projects
steps.text: Work from the prompt. The column names are in schema.sql.

questions.prompt: What shape does the result have?

choices.feedback: The query lists two columns, so only those two come back.
Two columns were asked for, and the table has one row per department.
A query without a filter returns every row of the table.

questions.prompt: What happens when you check this example?

choices.text: It returns the name column only.
choices.feedback: One bad name stops the whole statement. Nothing is returned.

choices.text: It returns both columns, with the second one empty.
choices.feedback: A column that does not exist is an error, not an empty column.

choices.text: PostgreSQL reports an error on line 1 and returns nothing.
choices.feedback: The misspelled column is on line 1, and the error names it (42703).

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise the SELECT list. They do not include reading and repairing an error.
